headline: Halfway Rock on the slack: cod holding deep, bass riding the mackerel push at Bailey
subhead: The bay's structure is doing what August structure does — cod tucked in the cold water, stripers and blues stacked wherever the mackerel decide to show.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning drifting off the back side of Peaks Island watching a raft of herring gulls work a bait ball no bigger than a rowboat, and it told me most of what I needed to know about this week. The mackerel are still here, but they're not the solid, mile-long schools we had in late May and June — they've broken into pockets, and you have to go find them rather than have them find you. That's a normal August transition, not a red flag, but it changes how you fish the bay.

Halfway Rock remains the anchor point for anyone serious about groundfish this week. I marked cod in 90 to 130 feet on the northwest side of the ledge, holding tight to bottom where the water stays coldest, and the pattern held true to what I'd expect for early August — you need the slack, or close to it, to get a clean vertical presentation down to them without your jig sailing off into the current. Diamond jigs in the 4- to 6-ounce range, tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked better than bare metal this week. Haddock were mixed in but scattered — I took two keeper-sized fish over three trips out there, which tells you this isn't a bang-bang bite right now. It's a patience bite. You put your time in on the slack, you cover the ledge methodically, and you take what the tide gives you.

The moon is sliding toward neap around August 5-6, and you can already feel the current softening at the Rock and out around Jewell Island. That's worth planning around. Weaker tidal push means groundfish spread out more over the structure instead of holding tight to the hardest current seams, so I'd widen my drift pattern rather than working the same six-foot lane over and over. It also means the window for a clean vertical jig stretches a little longer on either side of the actual slack, which is a small mercy if you're working the ledges solo.

Striped bass are doing exactly what I expected them to do this time of year — holding deep on structure through the warmest part of the day and coming up to feed hard at first light and again at dusk. I've had good reports of bass working the ledges off Cape Small and around the mouth of the New Meadows, chasing pogies and the scattered mackerel pods right at daybreak. Live-lined mackerel on a fish-finder rig is about as simple and effective as it gets out there, but if you don't want to run bait, a white bucktail with a chartreuse curl-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom on the last hour of the incoming, has been drawing strikes off Bailey Island near Mackerel Cove — appropriately enough. Daytime action has been tougher, mostly limited to guys jigging deep over structure at Ram Island Ledge and getting the occasional fish willing to commit in 40-plus feet of water.

Bluefish are the wild card this week. When they show, they show hard — I heard from a Harpswell captain who ran into a genuine blitz off Elm Island for about twenty minutes before it shut off as fast as it started. That's the nature of the bluefish right now: they're following bait, not holding structure, so you need to be mobile and ready to run when you see the birds working or the water start to nervous up. Metal lures — anything in the Hopkins or Kastmaster family — cast into the edge of a breaking school will get bit immediately if the fish are actually there.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions in the bay would hold steady through the week — and that's roughly what's happened. Nothing exploded, nothing collapsed. The bay is doing its normal early-August work: bait scattering, fish settling into low-light routines, groundfish tucking into the cold water on the ledges. It's an honest week, not a spectacular one.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the neap tide to soften current enough that Halfway Rock and Old Anthony's Ledge fish a little slower and a little wider through the weekend — lighter jigs, longer drifts, more patience required. For stripers, I'd focus my time on the dawn window at Cape Small and the Bailey Island ledges where mackerel have been showing, since that's where the bass are actually committing to feed. If the bluefish show again off Harpswell, treat it as a bonus, not a plan — they're moving too much right now to count on. Watch the wind through midweek; if it stays out of the southwest and light, the surface stays clean enough to sight-fish bait balls, which is half the game out here this time of year.
